Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

princess noun

also crown princess, king’s daughter

classical

Liv. 1.46.5: duae Tulliae rēgis fīliae
M-O s.v. princess

rēgis fīlia

noun phrase: fīlia with the genitive rēgis

a king’s daughter, a princess

As with prince, Latin says it with a phrase. Morgan–Owens adds prīncipissa, a medieval word, for a woman who rules a principality or a prince’s wife.

Other words

  • rēgīna, rēgīnae f. — a king’s daughter (in the poets); usually a queen

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Verg. A. 6.28 (Lewis & Short); Ov. Her. 12.1 (Lewis & Short); Curt. 3.12.21: virginēs rēgīnae (Lewis & Short)

    Of Ariadne and Medea in the poets, and of the daughters of Darius in Curtius (Lewis & Short); but a listener hears “queen” first (see queen).

  • rēgia virgo — a king’s daughter, a princess

    noun phrase: virgo with the adjective rēgia · also used · classical · Ov. Met. 2.570 (Lewis & Short, s.v. rēgius)

    (vōx poētica: Ov.)

Examples

  • hīs duōbus, ut ante dictum est, duae Tulliae rēgis fīliae nūpserant, et ipsae longē disparēs mōribus

    these two, as I said before, had married the two Tullias, the king’s daughters, who were themselves very different in characterLiv. 1.46.5

See also prince, queen, king, palace.

SourcesLewis & Short: rex · Lewis & Short: filia · Lewis & Short: regina · Lewis & Short: regius · Lewis & Short: virgo

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. princess.
